rows.source_statement: A process (X_t) on a metric space (T,d) has sub-gaussian increments when some K >= 0 satisfies ||X_t-X_s||_{psi_2} <= K d(t,s) for every t,s in T.
rows.next_foundation: Define sub-gaussian increments for a metric-indexed real random process, including the existential increment constant.

rows.source_statement: For all t,s in T, ||X_t-X_s||_{psi_2} <= K d(t,s).
rows.next_foundation: Establish the reusable Orlicz psi_2 increment predicate used by Definition 8.1.1.

rows.source_statement: For a Gaussian process, the canonical metric d(t,s) := ||X_t-X_s||_{L^2} makes the process have sub-gaussian increments with an absolute constant.
rows.next_foundation: Connect centered Gaussian L2 norms to psi_2 norms and prove the canonical metric increment bound.

rows.source_statement: A mean-zero process with K-sub-gaussian increments satisfies E sup_{t in T} X_t <= C K integral_0^infinity sqrt(log N(T,d,epsilon)) d epsilon.
rows.next_foundation: Build metric covering-number integration and the finite-process limiting reduction needed for Dudley’s integral bound.

rows.source_statement: A mean-zero process with K-sub-gaussian increments satisfies E sup_{t in T} X_t <= C K sum_{k in Z} 2^{-k} sqrt(log N(T,d,2^{-k})).
rows.next_foundation: Formalize finite dyadic nets and the chaining telescoping estimate underlying the discrete inequality.

rows.source_statement: E sup_{t in T} X_t <= C K sum_{k in Z} 2^{-k} sqrt(log N(T,d,2^{-k})).
rows.next_foundation: Prove the dyadic chaining sum after establishing finite epsilon-net selections.

rows.source_statement: For a closest point pi(t) in an epsilon-net, ||X_t-X_{pi(t)}||_{psi_2} <= K epsilon.
rows.next_foundation: Define a closest-net selector (or an approximate selector) and specialize the increment hypothesis.

rows.source_statement: The dyadic scale is epsilon_k = 2^{-k} for k in Z.
rows.next_foundation: Define the dyadic scale as a reusable real-valued sequence indexed by integers.

rows.source_statement: Choose epsilon_k-nets T_k with |T_k| = N(T,d,epsilon_k).
rows.next_foundation: Establish attainment or a finite approximate-net replacement for the covering-number minimum.

rows.source_statement: For finite T, choose integers kappa and K with T_kappa = {t_0} and T_K = T.
rows.next_foundation: Prove finite metric spaces admit coarsest singleton and finest exact nets at suitable dyadic scales.

rows.source_statement: For a closest point pi_k(t) in T_k, d(t,pi_k(t)) <= epsilon_k.
rows.next_foundation: Define the level-k net projection and prove its approximation inequality.

rows.source_statement: X_t-X_{t_0} is expanded as the full telescoping chain from pi_kappa(t) through pi_K(t).
rows.next_foundation: Prove the finite telescoping identity for the chain of net projections.

rows.source_statement: Because the endpoint terms vanish, X_t-X_{t_0} = sum_{k=kappa+1}^K (X_{pi_k(t)}-X_{pi_{k-1}(t)}).
rows.next_foundation: Discharge the endpoint identifications T_kappa={t_0} and T_K=T in the telescoping identity.

rows.source_statement: E sup_t (X_t-X_{t_0}) is at most the sum over k of E sup_t (X_{pi_k(t)}-X_{pi_{k-1}(t)}).
rows.next_foundation: Formalize the finite supremum-of-sum bound and expectation monotonicity.

rows.source_statement: Each chaining level satisfies E sup_t (X_{pi_k(t)}-X_{pi_{k-1}(t)}) <= C epsilon_{k-1} sqrt(log |T_k|).
rows.next_foundation: Instantiate the expected maximum bound for a finite family of sub-gaussian increments.

rows.source_statement: E sup_t (X_t-X_{t_0}) <= C sum_{k=kappa+1}^K epsilon_{k-1} sqrt(log |T_k|).
rows.next_foundation: Sum the levelwise increment bounds from Equation (8.11).

rows.source_statement: The chaining proof gives integral bounds for E sup_t |X_t-X_{t_0}| and E sup_{t,s} |X_t-X_s| without a mean-zero assumption.
rows.next_foundation: Generalize the Dudley proof to absolute increments about a base point and then apply the triangle inequality.

rows.source_statement: For every u >= 0, sup_{t,s} |X_t-X_s| <= C K [integral_0^infinity sqrt(log N(T,d,epsilon)) d epsilon + u diam(T)] with probability at least 1-2 exp(-u^2).
rows.next_foundation: Formalize the simultaneous high-probability chaining-level bounds requested in Exercise 8.1.7.

rows.source_statement: Prove Theorem 8.1.6 using high-probability versions of the chaining increment bound and a summable choice of level parameters z_k.
rows.next_foundation: First prove the finite-family tail maximum bound used at one chaining level.

rows.source_label: Exercise 8.1.8 (Equivalence of Dudley’s integral and sum)
rows.source_statement: Prove integral_0^infinity sqrt(log N(T,d,epsilon)) d epsilon <= C sum_{k in Z} 2^{-k} sqrt(log N(T,d,2^{-k})).
rows.next_foundation: Prove monotonicity of covering numbers and compare each dyadic integral interval to its endpoint.

rows.source_statement: Dudley’s integral may be truncated at diam(T), because one point is an epsilon-net whenever epsilon > diam(T).
rows.next_foundation: Prove the covering number is one above the diameter and truncate the entropy integral.

rows.source_statement: E sup_{t in T} X_t <= C K integral_0^{diam(T)} sqrt(log N(T,d,epsilon)) d epsilon.
rows.next_foundation: Specialize Dudley’s integral using vanishing metric entropy beyond diam(T).

rows.source_label: Theorem 8.1.10 (Dudley’s inequality for sets in R^n)
rows.source_statement: For every T subset R^n, w(T) <= C integral_0^infinity sqrt(log N(T,epsilon)) d epsilon.
rows.next_foundation: Instantiate Dudley’s theorem for the canonical Gaussian process and Euclidean metric.

rows.source_statement: The volumetric covering bound for the Euclidean unit ball gives w(B_2^n) <= C sqrt(n), which is optimal up to constants.
rows.next_foundation: Combine the unit-ball covering estimate with the Gaussian-width integral and evaluate the resulting scalar integral.

rows.source_statement: For T={e_k/sqrt(1+log k): k=1,...,n}, prove w(T) <= C.
rows.next_foundation: Apply the expected maximum bound to the Gaussian coordinates with their nonuniform scales.

rows.source_statement: For T={e_k/sqrt(1+log k): k=1,...,n}, prove the Dudley entropy integral diverges as n tends to infinity.
rows.next_foundation: Show the first m scaled basis vectors form a quantitatively separated packing and convert it to a covering lower bound.

rows.source_statement: For T subset R^n and s(T):=sup_{epsilon>=0} epsilon sqrt(log N(T,epsilon)), c s(T) <= w(T) <= C log(n) s(T).
rows.next_foundation: Formalize the truncated chaining proof, including the Gaussian residual bound at scale w(T)/(4 sqrt(n)).

rows.source_statement: The truncated chain gives w(T) <= sum_{k=kappa+1}^K E sup_t (X_{pi_k(t)}-X_{pi_{k-1}(t)}) + E sup_t (X_t-X_{pi_K(t)}).
rows.next_foundation: Repeat the chaining decomposition while retaining the nonzero terminal residual.

rows.source_statement: After bounding the residual by w(T)/2, w(T) <= 2 sum_{k=kappa+1}^K E sup_t (X_{pi_k(t)}-X_{pi_{k-1}(t)}).
rows.next_foundation: Prove and absorb the Gaussian terminal residual from Equation (8.14).

rows.source_statement: For T subset R^n, prove w(T) <= C integral_a^b sqrt(log N(T,epsilon)) d epsilon with a=c w(T)/sqrt(n) and b=diam(T).
rows.next_foundation: Combine the upper truncation at the diameter with the lower-scale residual estimate from Theorem 8.1.13.

rows.source_statement: If X has law mu, then integral_Omega f dmu = E f(X).
rows.next_foundation: Formalize the law/pushforward integration identity with the required measurability and integrability conditions.

rows.source_statement: For iid copies X_i of X, (1/n) sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i) tends almost surely to E f(X).
rows.next_foundation: Instantiate the strong law for the integrable random variables f(X_i).

rows.source_statement: The Monte-Carlo display writes integral f dmu approximately equal to (1/n) sum_i f(X_i).
rows.reason: Equation (8.17) uses an unquantified approximation sign and asserts no fixed error, mode of convergence, or probability. Equation (8.16) and Remark 8.2.1 carry its precise convergence content.

rows.source_statement: The expected absolute Monte-Carlo error is O(1/sqrt(n)), via the variance of the sample average.
rows.next_foundation: State the finite-variance assumptions and derive the L1 error from the sample-mean variance identity.

rows.source_statement: E |(1/n) sum_i f(X_i)-E f(X)| <= sqrt(Var((1/n) sum_i f(X_i))) = O(1/sqrt(n)).
rows.next_foundation: Formalize the Cauchy-Schwarz L1/L2 step and independent sample-mean variance formula.

rows.source_statement: Monte-Carlo integration requires only the ability to sample from mu and evaluate f at the sampled points, not a closed form for mu or values of f everywhere.
rows.next_foundation: Model the sampling-oracle and point-evaluation content separately from the mathematical convergence theorem.
Define the Lipschitz hypothesis class with its supremum-metric structure.

rows.source_statement: For iid [0,1]-valued X,X_1,...,X_n and F the L-Lipschitz real functions, E sup_{f in F} |(1/n)sum_i f(X_i)-E f(X)| <= C L/sqrt(n).
rows.next_foundation: Develop the empirical-process increment bound and covering entropy of the Lipschitz class.

rows.source_statement: E sup_{f in F} |(1/n)sum_i f(X_i)-E f(X)| <= C L/sqrt(n).
rows.next_foundation: Combine Dudley’s inequality with a convergent covering-entropy integral for F.

rows.source_statement: With high probability one sample approximates every f in F at the same O(L/sqrt(n)) rate as the single-function law of large numbers.
rows.next_foundation: Apply Markov’s inequality to the nonnegative supremum error and state the resulting probability/error tradeoff.

rows.source_statement: For a function class F and iid sample, the empirical process is X_f := (1/n)sum_i f(X_i)-E f(X), indexed by f in F.
rows.next_foundation: Define the empirical process as a random function on the index class with measurable finite-sample averages.

rows.source_statement: X_f := (1/n) sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i)-E f(X).
rows.next_foundation: Implement the empirical-process coordinate definition.

rows.source_statement: For the proof it suffices to use F := {f:[0,1]->[0,1] : ||f||_Lip <= 1}.
rows.next_foundation: Prove the centering, rescaling, and range-normalization reduction from general L.

rows.source_statement: For f,g in the normalized Lipschitz class, ||X_f-X_g||_{psi_2} is at most an absolute constant times ||f-g||_infinity/sqrt(n).
rows.next_foundation: Combine independence, centering in psi_2, and bounded-variable sub-gaussian estimates.

rows.source_statement: For the normalized one-dimensional Lipschitz class, N(F,||.||_infinity,epsilon) <= (C/epsilon)^(C/epsilon).
rows.next_foundation: Construct mesh-following approximants and count them.

rows.source_label: Exercise 8.2.6 (Metric entropy of the class of Lipschitz functions)
rows.source_statement: For F={f:[0,1]->[0,1]: ||f||_Lip<=1}, prove N(F,||.||_infinity,epsilon) <= (2/epsilon)^(2/epsilon) for epsilon in (0,1).
rows.next_foundation: Formalize the square mesh, mesh-following approximation, and its finite cardinality bound.

rows.source_label: Exercise 8.2.7 (An improved bound on the metric entropy)
rows.source_statement: Improve the preceding estimate to N(F,||.||_infinity,epsilon) <= exp(C/epsilon) for every epsilon>0.
rows.next_foundation: Exploit the Lipschitz restriction to bound the branching choices of successive mesh values.

rows.source_statement: For anchored 1-Lipschitz f:[0,1]^d->R under the infinity metric, prove N(F,||.||_infinity,epsilon) <= exp(C/epsilon^d) for epsilon>0.
rows.next_foundation: Build a finite cube mesh and a Lipschitz-consistent extension/counting argument in dimension d.

rows.source_statement: The empirical measure is described by mu_n({X_i})=1/n for every i=1,...,n.
rows.next_foundation: Resolve repeated sample points explicitly and define mu_n as (1/n) times the sum of Dirac measures before auditing the printed singleton formula.

rows.source_statement: The random probability measure uniformly supported on the sample X_1,...,X_n is called the empirical measure mu_n.
rows.next_foundation: Define mu_n as the normalized finite sum of Dirac measures so repeated sample values retain their multiplicities.

rows.source_label: Section 8.2.3 body: population and empirical expectations
rows.source_statement: The notation is mu f = integral f dmu = E f(X) and mu_n f = integral f dmu_n = (1/n)sum_i f(X_i).
rows.next_foundation: Prove the integration formula for the finite empirical measure, including multiplicities.

rows.source_statement: The printed body states X_f = mu f - mu_n f, whereas Definition 8.2.5 and Equation (8.21) define X_f = mu_n f - mu f.
rows.next_foundation: Audit the printed sign inconsistency and choose a source-facing correction while preserving the absolute-deviation results.

rows.source_statement: The uniform law controls the quantity E sup_{f in F} |mu_n f-mu f|.
rows.next_foundation: Rewrite Equation (8.20) using empirical-measure integration.

rows.source_statement: The text identifies the Lipschitz-function supremum deviation with the Wasserstein distance W_1(mu,mu_n).
rows.next_foundation: State the exact unit-Lipschitz dual definition, separate the random distance from its expectation, and audit the class normalization.

rows.source_statement: The text states that the Lipschitz dual expression is equivalent to the transportation-cost formulation of W_1.
rows.next_foundation: Locate or develop the measure-theoretic hypotheses and exact Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality needed for the source-facing bridge.

rows.source_statement: A subset Lambda is shattered by a Boolean class F if every Boolean function on Lambda is a restriction of some f in F; vc(F) is the largest cardinality of a shattered subset, or infinity when none is largest.
rows.next_foundation: Define restriction-surjectivity shattering and extended-natural VC dimension.

rows.source_statement: The class of indicators of closed intervals in R has VC dimension 2.
rows.next_foundation: Exhibit a shattered two-point set and prove every ordered three-point set has an unrealizable 1,0,1 labeling.

rows.source_statement: The class of indicators of closed half-planes in R^2 has VC dimension 3.
rows.next_foundation: Formalize shattering of three points in general position and the obstruction for every four-point configuration, including degeneracies.

rows.source_statement: For Omega={1,2,3} and F={001,010,100,111}, the class has VC dimension 2.
rows.next_foundation: Enumerate restrictions to a shattered two-point subset and show the full three-point set is not shattered.

rows.source_statement: Indicators of unions [a,b] union [c,d] in R have VC dimension 4.
rows.next_foundation: Characterize label alternations on ordered finite subsets of R.

rows.source_statement: Indicators of circles in R^2 have VC dimension 3.
rows.next_foundation: Prove a three-point shattering construction and a four-point obstruction using planar circle geometry.

rows.source_statement: Indicators of closed axis-aligned rectangles in R^2 have VC dimension 4.
rows.next_foundation: Exhibit four shattered points and prove a five-point obstruction via coordinate extrema.

rows.source_statement: Indicators of closed axis-aligned squares in R^2 have VC dimension 3.
rows.next_foundation: Exhibit a three-point shattering configuration and prove no four points are shattered.

rows.source_statement: Indicators of unrestricted convex polygons in R^2 have infinite VC dimension.
rows.next_foundation: Construct arbitrarily large finite sets in convex position and realize every subset by a convex polygon.

rows.source_label: Remark 8.3.10 (VC dimension of classes of sets)
rows.source_statement: VC dimension for Boolean-function classes agrees with VC dimension for the corresponding classes of one-sets; intervals have value 2 and half-planes value 3.
rows.next_foundation: Prove the bijective correspondence between subsets and indicator functions preserves restriction and shattering.

rows.source_statement: Give the definition of VC dimension directly for a class of subsets of Omega.
rows.next_foundation: Define set-family shattering by realizing every trace on a finite subset and prove equivalence to the indicator formulation.

rows.source_statement: The text states VC dimensions 7 for all planar rectangles, 2k+1 for planar k-vertex polygons, and n+1 for half-spaces in R^n.
rows.next_foundation: Separate the three asserted families and establish reusable upper/lower VC-dimension arguments for each.

rows.source_statement: For a finite Boolean class, |F| >= 2^{vc(F)}.
rows.next_foundation: Use restriction surjectivity on a shattered set to inject all Boolean labelings into F.

rows.source_statement: For a Boolean class F on a finite set Omega, |F| is at most the number of subsets of Omega shattered by F, including the empty set.
rows.next_foundation: Formalize the induction splitting F by the value at one point and the double-counting repair Lambda -> Lambda union {x_0}.

rows.source_statement: For the split classes F_0 and F_1, S(F_0)>=|F_0| and S(F_1)>=|F_1| by induction.
rows.next_foundation: Apply the induction hypothesis to the restrictions of F_0 and F_1 to Omega without x_0.

rows.source_statement: The shattered-set count satisfies S(F) >= S(F_0)+S(F_1).
rows.next_foundation: Construct an injection accounting for sets shattered by both subclasses using adjoining x_0.

rows.source_statement: For F={001,010,100,111}, the Pajor induction split at coordinate 3 has S(F_0)=S(F_1)=2 and adjoining coordinate 3 supplies two additional shattered subsets.
rows.next_foundation: Enumerate the two split classes and their shattered traces.

rows.source_statement: Prove Pajor’s Lemma is sharp using binary strings of length n with at most d ones.
rows.next_foundation: Prove the shattered subsets are exactly those of cardinality at most d and count both sides.

rows.source_statement: For a Boolean class F on an n-point set and d=vc(F), |F| <= sum_{k=0}^d binom(n,k) <= (e n/d)^d.
rows.next_foundation: Combine Pajor’s lemma with the cardinality bound on shattered sets and the binomial-sum estimate.

rows.source_statement: Show the Sauer-Shelah bound is sharp for every n and d.
rows.next_foundation: Use the Hamming ball of binary strings with at most d ones and compute its VC dimension and cardinality.

rows.source_statement: For Boolean f,g, d(f,g):=||f-g||_{L^2(mu)}=(integral |f-g|^2 dmu)^{1/2}; covering numbers are denoted N(F,L^2(mu),epsilon).
rows.next_foundation: Define the pseudometric quotient or record the pseudometric convention needed by covering numbers.

rows.source_statement: For a Boolean class F on a probability space and epsilon in (0,1), N(F,L^2(mu),epsilon) <= (2/epsilon)^{C d}, where d=vc(F).
rows.next_foundation: Develop the finite separated-subclass reduction, Lemma 8.3.19, and Sauer-Shelah cardinality estimate.

rows.source_statement: If |Omega|=n and d=vc(F), then N(F,L^2(mu),epsilon) <= |F| <= (e n/d)^d.
rows.next_foundation: Apply Sauer-Shelah to the finite restriction and bound any covering number by class cardinality.

rows.source_statement: For N Boolean functions that are pairwise epsilon-separated in L^2(mu), some n <= C epsilon^{-4} log N and n-point Omega_n make all restrictions pairwise distinct.
rows.next_foundation: Formalize iid coordinate sampling, Hoeffding concentration, and a union bound over function pairs.

rows.source_statement: For sampled X_1,...,X_n, ||f-g||_{L^2(mu_n)}^2 := (1/n) sum_i (f-g)(X_i)^2.
rows.next_foundation: Define the multiplicity-aware empirical measure and prove its finite-sum integration formula.

rows.source_statement: With probability at least 1-2 exp(-c n epsilon^4), ||f-g||_{L^2(mu_n)}^2 >= ||f-g||_{L^2(mu)}^2-epsilon^2/4 >= 3 epsilon^2/4.
rows.next_foundation: Apply Hoeffding to h=(f-g)^2 and use the epsilon-separation assumption.

rows.source_statement: After a union bound over at most N^2 pairs, the simultaneous event has probability at least 1-N^2*2 exp(-c n epsilon^4).
rows.next_foundation: Formalize the finite pair union bound and choose n so the lower bound is positive.

rows.source_statement: Lemma 8.3.19 and Johnson-Lindenstrauss both reduce N points to dimension O(log N) while preserving geometry, but use coordinate sampling versus a uniform random subspace.
rows.next_foundation: Make the two target notions of geometry and projection explicit before formulating a precise comparison.

rows.source_statement: For functions bounded by 1 and epsilon in (0,1), find n <= C epsilon^{-4} log N(F,L^2(mu),epsilon) and Omega_n with N(F,L^2(mu),epsilon) <= N(F,L^2(mu_n),epsilon/4).
rows.next_foundation: Adapt Lemma 8.3.19 to a maximal separated set and apply the covering-packing relationship.

rows.source_statement: Determine the covering-number bound corresponding to Theorem 8.3.18 for epsilon >= 1.
rows.next_foundation: Use the diameter of Boolean functions in L^2 of a probability measure to show when one center suffices.

rows.source_statement: For a Boolean class F of finite VC dimension at least 1 and iid X_i, E sup_{f in F} [(1/n)sum_i f(X_i)-E f(X)] <= C sqrt(vc(F)/n).
rows.next_foundation: Combine symmetrization, conditional sub-gaussian increments, Dudley’s inequality, and the VC covering bound.

rows.source_statement: E sup_{f in F} [(1/n)sum_i f(X_i)-E f(X)] <= C sqrt(vc(F)/n).
rows.next_foundation: Complete the conditional Dudley integral after bounding L^2(mu_n) covering numbers by VC dimension.

rows.source_statement: Prove E sup_f [(1/n)sum_i f(X_i)-E f(X)] <= 2 E sup_f (1/n)sum_i epsilon_i f(X_i) for independent symmetric Bernoulli signs.
rows.next_foundation: Adapt Symmetrization Lemma 6.4.2 to the supremum over the function class.

rows.source_statement: Conditionally on the sample, (2/sqrt(n)) E sup_f Z_f is bounded by (1/sqrt(n)) E integral_0^1 sqrt(log N(F,L^2(mu_n),epsilon)) d epsilon up to an absolute constant.
rows.next_foundation: Apply the increment form of Dudley’s inequality to the Rademacher process Z_f.

rows.source_statement: Bound E sup_{f in F}|Z_f| in the proof of Theorem 8.3.23 after only E sup_f Z_f was bounded.
rows.next_foundation: Adjoin the zero function, use the supremum-of-increments bound, and control the VC-dimension change.

rows.source_statement: For a real random variable X, F(x):=P{X<=x}.
rows.next_foundation: Use the measurable lower-ray event to define the cumulative distribution function.

rows.source_statement: For a sample X_1,...,X_n, F_n(x):=#{i in [n]: X_i<=x}/n.
rows.next_foundation: Define the finite empirical CDF and connect it to averages of lower-ray indicators.

rows.source_statement: For every x in R, E|F_n(x)-F(x)| <= C/sqrt(n).
rows.next_foundation: Compute the variance of lower-ray indicator variables and apply the L1/L2 bound.

rows.source_statement: For independent real random variables with common CDF F, E ||F_n-F||_infinity <= C/sqrt(n).
rows.next_foundation: Instantiate Theorem 8.3.23 with indicators of lower half-lines and verify their VC dimension bound.

rows.source_statement: For iid uniform points in [0,1]^2, with high probability every circle C has #sample-points-in-C = Area(C)*n + O(sqrt(n)); the same holds for any bounded-VC geometric class listed.
rows.next_foundation: Derive a quantified high-probability deviation from Theorem 8.3.23 for the class of circle indicators.

rows.source_statement: A real-valued class F is uniform Glivenko-Cantelli when for every epsilon>0, lim_{n->infinity} sup_mu P{sup_{f in F}[(1/n)sum_i f(X_i)-E f(X)]>epsilon}=0; finite-VC Boolean classes have this property.
rows.next_foundation: Define the uniform-in-law convergence property and apply Markov’s inequality to Theorem 8.3.23.

rows.source_statement: Prove that a Boolean class with infinite VC dimension is not uniform Glivenko-Cantelli.
rows.next_foundation: Choose arbitrarily large shattered finite sets with uniform measures and construct a sample-dependent labeling.

rows.source_statement: Use Sauer-Shelah directly to prove Equation (8.29) with C sqrt((d/n) log(e n/d)) for d=vc(F).
rows.next_foundation: Condition on the sample, reduce to the finite trace class, and combine concentration with a union bound and Sauer-Shelah.

rows.source_statement: Training data consist of (X_i,T(X_i)) for i=1,...,n.
rows.next_foundation: Define a supervised training sample from iid inputs and a deterministic target function.

rows.source_statement: A classification problem is a learning problem whose target function is Boolean, so it assigns every point to one of two classes.
rows.next_foundation: Define the Boolean supervised-learning specialization independently of the concrete health-study example.

rows.source_statement: A Boolean target T:R^d->{0,1} models diagnosis from d health parameters, with labeled patient vectors as training data.
rows.next_foundation: Instantiate the classification framework with a Euclidean feature space and Boolean labels.

rows.source_statement: The squared-loss population risk is R(f):=E (f(X)-T(X))^2.
rows.next_foundation: Define population squared-loss risk with the needed measurability and integrability assumptions.

rows.source_statement: For Boolean target and predictor, R(f)=P{f(X) != T(X)}.
rows.next_foundation: Prove the squared Boolean difference equals the misclassification indicator pointwise and integrate.

rows.source_statement: For Boolean f and T, R(f)=P{f(X) != T(X)}.
rows.next_foundation: Formalize the pointwise Boolean-loss identity and probability conversion.

rows.source_statement: Assuming the minimum is attained, f* := argmin_{f in F} R(f).
rows.next_foundation: Represent an attained risk minimizer without relying on a noncomputable argmin notation lacking an existence witness.

rows.source_statement: A hypothesis space F is the prescribed class of candidate predictors in which the learned solution f must lie.
rows.next_foundation: Package the candidate class and membership condition used by population-risk and empirical-risk minimizers.

rows.source_statement: The empirical risk is R_n(f):=(1/n)sum_i (f(X_i)-T(X_i))^2, and f_n* is an empirical-risk minimizer over F.
rows.next_foundation: Define empirical squared risk and package an attained minimizer with its membership and optimality properties.
Define the empirical squared-risk finite average.

rows.source_statement: The excess risk caused by learning from n samples is R(f_n*)-R(f*).
rows.next_foundation: Define excess risk from the selected population and empirical minimizers.

rows.source_statement: For a Boolean target and Boolean hypothesis class F with finite vc(F)>=1, E R(f_n*) <= R(f*) + C sqrt(vc(F)/n).
rows.next_foundation: Reduce excess risk to uniform deviations and transfer the VC covering estimate from F to the loss class.

rows.source_statement: Pointwise, R(f_n*)-R(f*) <= 2 sup_{f in F}|R_n(f)-R(f)|.
rows.next_foundation: Use empirical optimality of f_n* and insert/subtract empirical risks.

rows.source_statement: The expected uniform risk deviation is written as E sup_{ell in L} [(1/n)sum_i ell(X_i)-E ell(X)] for L={(f-T)^2:f in F}.
rows.next_foundation: Rewrite empirical-minus-population risk using the induced Boolean loss class.

rows.source_statement: The proof bounds the uniform deviation by (1/sqrt(n)) E integral_0^1 sqrt(log N(L,L^2(mu_n),epsilon)) d epsilon up to an absolute constant.
rows.next_foundation: Apply symmetrization and conditional Dudley chaining to the loss class.

rows.source_statement: For Boolean f,g,T and epsilon in (0,1), N(L,L^2(mu_n),epsilon) <= N(F,L^2(mu_n),epsilon).
rows.next_foundation: Prove the loss transform is an isometry on Boolean functions using the pointwise identity in Exercise 8.4.6.

rows.source_statement: Check Equation (8.37), using ((f-T)^2-(g-T)^2)^2=(f-g)^2 for Boolean f,g,T.
rows.next_foundation: Prove the Boolean pointwise identity and map every epsilon-net of F to an epsilon-net of the loss class.

rows.source_statement: To make expected excess risk at most epsilon, it suffices up to constants to take n asymptotic to epsilon^{-2} vc(F).
rows.next_foundation: Solve Theorem 8.4.4’s deviation term for n and state the approximation-risk contribution separately.

rows.source_statement: For the worked planar example, F:={1_C : circles C subset R^2}.
rows.next_foundation: Define the circle-indicator hypothesis class and connect it to Exercise 8.3.6.

rows.source_statement: Show f_n* minimizes the number of sample points on which f disagrees with the labels T(X_i).
rows.next_foundation: Rewrite Boolean empirical squared loss as the misclassification count divided by n.

rows.source_statement: Extend the theory through Theorem 8.4.4 to iid training pairs (X_i,Y_i) where Y is random and correlated with X.
rows.next_foundation: Redefine population and empirical risks on the joint input-output law and reprove the uniform-deviation reduction.

rows.source_label: Exercise 8.4.9 (Learning in the class of Lipschitz functions)
rows.source_statement: For L-Lipschitz f:[0,1]->[0,1], prove ||X_f-X_g||_{psi_2} <= C(L)||f-g||_infinity/sqrt(n) for X_f=R_n(f)-R(f).
rows.next_foundation: Bound the centered difference of squared losses pointwise and apply the independent-sum psi_2 estimate.

rows.source_label: Exercise 8.4.9 (Learning in the class of Lipschitz functions)
rows.source_statement: Use Dudley’s inequality to prove E sup_{f in F}|R_n(f)-R(f)| <= C(L)/sqrt(n).
rows.next_foundation: Combine part (a) with the one-dimensional Lipschitz-class entropy bound.

rows.source_label: Exercise 8.4.9 (Learning in the class of Lipschitz functions)
rows.source_statement: Conclude E[R(f_n*)-R(f*)] <= C(L)/sqrt(n).
rows.next_foundation: Apply Lemma 8.4.5 to the uniform-risk bound from part (b).

rows.source_statement: The earlier chaining argument gives E sup_t X_t <= C sum_{k=kappa+1}^infinity epsilon_{k-1} sqrt(log |T_k|).
rows.next_foundation: Extract the general-scale form of the Dudley chaining estimate.

rows.source_statement: An admissible sequence satisfies |T_0|=1 and |T_k| <= 2^(2^k) for k>=1.
rows.next_foundation: Define admissible sequences of finite subsets with the double-exponential cardinality bound.

rows.source_label: Section 8.5.1 footnote: distance to a subset
rows.source_statement: For t in a metric space and A subset T, d(t,A):=inf{d(t,a):a in A}.
rows.next_foundation: Use the metric infimum definition and specify behavior for empty sets; admissible approximating sets are nonempty.

rows.source_statement: After choosing epsilon_k=sup_t d(t,T_k) and reindexing, E sup_t X_t <= C sum_{k=0}^infinity 2^(k/2) sup_t d(t,T_k).
rows.next_foundation: Substitute admissible cardinality bounds into Equation (8.39) and reindex the series.

rows.source_statement: gamma_2(T,d):=inf over admissible (T_k) of sup_{t in T} sum_{k=0}^infinity 2^(k/2) d(t,T_k).
rows.next_foundation: Define admissible sequences and the extended-real infimum/supremum series underlying gamma_2.

rows.source_statement: For T={0} union {e_k/sqrt(1+log k):k=1,...,n}, prove gamma_2(T,d)<=C.
rows.next_foundation: Construct T_k from the first 2^(2^k) basis vectors and bound each point’s chaining sum.

rows.source_statement: For the same T, prove inf_{admissible (T_k)} sum_k 2^(k/2) sup_t d(t,T_k) tends to infinity with n.
rows.next_foundation: Relate each admissible cardinality level to a tail vector omitted from T_k and sum the resulting lower bounds.

rows.source_statement: A mean-zero process with K-sub-gaussian increments satisfies E sup_{t in T} X_t <= C K gamma_2(T,d).
rows.next_foundation: Formalize the admissible-sequence chaining proof and take the infimum over sequences.

rows.source_statement: For an admissible sequence, choose pi_k(t) in T_k with d(t,pi_k(t))=d(t,T_k).
rows.next_foundation: Establish existence for finite nonempty T_k or formulate an approximation robust to unattained infima.

rows.source_statement: For a finite chain ending at t, X_t-X_{t_0}=sum_{k=1}^K (X_{pi_k(t)}-X_{pi_{k-1}(t)}).
rows.next_foundation: Prove the generic-chain telescoping identity.

rows.source_statement: The proof says one would like a high-probability simultaneous inequality X_{pi_k(t)}-X_{pi_{k-1}(t)} <= 2^(k/2)d(t,T_k).
rows.reason: Equation (8.43) is introduced as a desired heuristic shape, with no probability level or absolute constant. The actual quantified bound is Equation (8.44), which remains an actionable row.

rows.source_statement: For fixed k,t and u>=0, X_{pi_k(t)}-X_{pi_{k-1}(t)} <= C u 2^(k/2)d(pi_k(t),pi_{k-1}(t)) with probability at least 1-2 exp(-8u^2 2^k).
rows.next_foundation: Convert the psi_2 increment estimate to a tail inequality with explicit rescaled constants.

rows.source_statement: On the simultaneous event, |X_t-X_{t_0}| <= C u sum_{k=1}^infinity 2^(k/2)d(pi_k(t),pi_{k-1}(t)).
rows.next_foundation: Sum the simultaneous increment bounds along the telescoping chain.

rows.source_label: Section 8.5.2 body: gamma_2 supremum norm bound
rows.source_statement: The proof obtains ||sup_{t in T}|X_t-X_{t_0}|||_{psi_2} <= C gamma_2(T,d).
rows.next_foundation: Translate the proved sub-gaussian tail bound for the supremum into the psi_2 norm estimate.

rows.source_statement: Without a mean-zero assumption, E sup_{t,s in T}|X_t-X_s| <= C K gamma_2(T,d).
rows.next_foundation: Apply generic chaining to a process based at t_0 and use the triangle inequality.

rows.source_statement: For every u>=0, sup_{t,s}|X_t-X_s| <= C K[gamma_2(T,d)+u diam(T)] with probability at least 1-2 exp(-u^2).
rows.next_foundation: Implement the modified increment bound and lazy-walk construction requested by Exercise 8.5.6.

rows.source_statement: Prove Theorem 8.5.5 using increments scaled by u+2^(k/2) and a lazy walk whose total metric step length is geometrically bounded.
rows.next_foundation: Formalize the lazy subsequence selection when distance to t drops by a factor of two.

rows.source_statement: For every metric space, gamma_2(T,d) <= C integral_0^infinity sqrt(log N(T,d,epsilon)) d epsilon.
rows.next_foundation: Construct an admissible sequence from near-minimal nets at entropy thresholds 2^(2^k).

rows.source_statement: For a mean-zero Gaussian process with canonical metric d(t,s)=||X_t-X_s||_{L^2}, c gamma_2(T,d) <= E sup_t X_t <= C gamma_2(T,d).
rows.next_foundation: Reuse the generic-chaining upper bound and identify an authorized formal foundation for Talagrand’s unproved lower bound.

rows.source_statement: If X is mean-zero, Y is mean-zero Gaussian, and ||X_t-X_s||_{psi_2} <= K||Y_t-Y_s||_{L^2}, then E sup_t X_t <= C K E sup_t Y_t.
rows.next_foundation: Apply generic chaining to X in Y’s canonical metric and the lower half of Theorem 8.6.1.

rows.source_statement: For Y_x=<g,x> on T subset R^n, w(T)=E sup_{x in T}<g,x>.
rows.next_foundation: Connect the existing Gaussian-width definition to the canonical Gaussian process used here.

rows.source_statement: For a mean-zero process on T subset R^n with ||X_x-X_y||_{psi_2} <= K||x-y||_2, E sup_{x in T}X_x <= C K w(T).
rows.next_foundation: Instantiate Corollary 8.6.2 with the canonical Gaussian process <g,x>.

rows.source_statement: If X_0=0 and increments on T union {0} obey ||X_x-X_y||_{psi_2}<=K||x-y||_2, prove E sup_{x in T}|X_x| <= C K gamma(T).
rows.next_foundation: Combine Remark 8.5.4, majorizing measure, and the Gaussian-width-to-complexity comparison.

rows.source_statement: Under Exercise 8.6.4’s assumptions, prove sup_{x in T}|X_x| <= C K[w(T)+u rad(T)] with probability at least 1-2 exp(-u^2).
rows.next_foundation: Apply Theorem 8.5.5 to T union {0} and translate gamma_2 and diameter to width and radius.

rows.source_statement: Under Exercise 8.6.4’s assumptions, prove (E sup_{x in T}|X_x|^p)^(1/p) <= C sqrt(p) K gamma(T).
rows.next_foundation: Integrate the sub-gaussian tail bound or apply the psi_2-to-L^p moment comparison.

rows.source_statement: The target random quadratic form is sup_{x in T,y in S}<A x,y>.
rows.next_foundation: Define the indexed bilinear random process on T times S.

rows.source_statement: rad(T):=sup_{x in T}||x||_2.
rows.next_foundation: Define Euclidean radius for bounded subsets, with an extended-real convention if needed.

rows.source_statement: For an m by n matrix with independent mean-zero sub-gaussian entries, E sup_{x in T,y in S}<Ax,y> <= C K[w(T)rad(S)+w(S)rad(T)], K=max_ij||A_ij||_{psi_2}.
rows.next_foundation: Prove the bilinear process increment bound and compare it with the sum of two independent canonical Gaussian processes.

rows.source_statement: Taking T=S^{n-1} and S=S^{m-1} yields E||A|| <= C K(sqrt(n)+sqrt(m)).
rows.next_foundation: Identify the bilinear supremum with operator norm and use Gaussian widths and unit radii of Euclidean spheres.

rows.source_statement: For iid standard Gaussian entries, prove E sup_{x in T,y in S}<Ax,y> >= c[w(T)rad(S)+w(S)rad(T)].
rows.next_foundation: Lower-bound separately after fixing an almost-maximal-radius x and y, then combine the two bounds.

rows.source_statement: Under Theorem 8.7.1’s assumptions, prove a tail bound for sup_{x in T,y in S}<Ax,y>.
rows.next_foundation: Apply Exercise 8.6.5 to the bilinear process using the product-space increment metric.

rows.source_statement: For iid N(0,1) entries, prove E sup_{x in T,y in S}<Ax,y> <= w(T)rad(S)+w(S)rad(T) with sharp constant 1.
rows.next_foundation: Use the exact Gaussian increment comparison and Sudakov-Fernique rather than the sub-gaussian comparison constant.
